1.pericope_label: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty... He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler

schools.summary: Delitzsch and Ellicott work from date, position and idiom: the psalm stands here for a verbal link with the one before, and its images are drawn from fowling, the eagle's wing and the Eastern plague.

Gill and Calvin press the security of the covenant relation, Gill locating the secret place in God's own heart and Calvin rebuking those who profess providence but will not entrust their safety to it.
Clarke and Wesley handle the text soberly, Clarke collecting the manuscript and version evidence and Wesley reducing the condition to making God one's habitation.
Henry and Spurgeon divide over reach: Henry states the promise for all who live in communion with God, Spurgeon reserves it for those who habitually dwell in the inner sanctuary.
Augustine reads the psalm through the temptation of Christ, treating it as armour against the devil's hidden assault rather than open persecution.

debates.question: Who is speaking in the second verse, and is the psalm one voice or a dialogue?

positions.summary: The psalmist speaks it himself, though the ancient versions put the words in the mouth of the man who dwells in the secret place.
A tradition makes the psalm a dialogue, David asserting the first verse, Solomon answering, David replying with the promises, and God speaking at the close.
One voice throughout, and a pointed one: I will say of the Lord whatever others say of him.

debates.question: Are the opening promises for every believer or only for those in close fellowship?

positions.summary: Only for those who habitually dwell in the most holy place; others run to it at times without residing there.
For all who live in communion with God, who have not merely admittance but residence.
Stated generally, but with the complaint that few who profess providence will actually entrust their safety to it.

outliers.summary: Frames the entire psalm by the devil's use of it against Christ, making it armour for the hidden assault rather than the open persecution.
Rejects as forced the construction that joins the first three verses into a single sentence, holding that the clauses state distinct ideas.

themes: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
I will say of the Lord, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.
Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence.
He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.

5.pericope_label: Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day... Because thou hast made the Lord, which is my refuge, even the most High, thy habitation

schools.summary: Delitzsch and Ellicott read the perils as climate and idiom and resolve the ninth verse by construction, Ellicott proposing an under-soliloquy where the Authorised Version does violence to the text.
Gill draws out the plague at length and settles the ninth verse from the accents, insisting the thousands fall by pestilence rather than battle.
Clarke reports the Chaldee's night demons and a rendering that makes the fallen thousands enemies; Wesley keeps the terms general.
Henry expounds the character of the man who makes God his habitation; Spurgeon leaves exposition for the 1854 cholera and what the verse did for him.

debates.question: How should the change of person in the ninth verse be resolved?

positions.summary: The Authorised Version avoids the difficulty only by violence to the text; the first line is an under-soliloquy in which the poet breaks off to say this is true of himself.
The accents require because thou, Lord, art my refuge, leaving open whether the words are the good man's or the psalmist's.
Read straight through as addressed to the man who has taken the Most High for his portion.

debates.question: Is the thousand falling at one's side a battle or a plague?

positions.summary: The pestilence just described, not battle.
Reports a rendering that makes them enemies falling on either side without coming near enough to take his life.
Leaves it open: the night terror may be an enemy attack, or the arrow may be the Eastern name for the plague, which Arabians still call God's arrow.

debates.question: Are the four perils of the passage personal agents or natural evils?

positions.summary: Records the Chaldee's demons that walk by night and the rabbinic division of death's empire between a day demon and a noonday destroyer.
Climate and idiom only: night and noon are the unwholesome hours in the East, and the word for destruction means by parallelism a deadly sickness.
The plague itself, terrible at a distance and worse by night, when the dead are carried out.

outliers.summary: Abandons exposition at the ninth verse for the 1854 cholera in his London parish, and the verse pasted in a shoemaker's window that ended his sinking.

themes: Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day;
Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness; nor for the destruction that wasteth at noonday.
A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee.
Only with thine eyes shalt thou behold and see the reward of the wicked.
Because thou hast made the Lord, which is my refuge, even the most High, thy habitation;

10.pericope_label: There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling... With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation

schools.summary: Ellicott ties the promise to the conditions laid down just before, denies that the verse originated the guardian angel, and closes on the fitness of long life to a psalm about dangers to life.

Gill qualifies the promise by distinguishing chastisement from punishment, takes the lion and adder for Satan under two figures, and argues from the temptation that the received sense of the verse is the true one.
Clarke makes the path of duty the way of safety, cautions against praying to angels, and turns to natural history for the asp; Wesley extends the creatures to all pernicious beasts and enemies.
Spurgeon reads the clause as no restriction to a heart right with God and gives the believer the whole bodyguard of heaven rather than a single angel.

debates.question: Is the promised protection conditional on the man's conduct?

positions.summary: Strictly conditional: the path of duty is the way of safety, and no man can expect protection who does not walk in obedience.
No restriction to a heart right with God, since it is not the believer's way to go out of his way.
The angels are charged with the care of all who fulfil the conditions laid down just before.

debates.question: What are the lion and the adder?

positions.summary: Literally savage creatures, then figuratively Satan under two figures, a lion for cruelty and a serpent for craft.
Emblems of the dangers that threaten life generally.
All pernicious creatures and all sorts of enemies.
Takes them as natural history, the asp a small serpent of Egypt and Libya whose poison kills without remedy.

debates.question: Does the guardianship of the angels support a personal guardian angel?

positions.summary: No: not one guardian angel but the whole bodyguard of heaven.
No: the notion originated in heathen belief and was only encouraged by this verse.
No, and the charge given them proves they are not to be prayed to nor praised, but God only.

outliers.summary: Argues that Satan's use of the verse against Christ establishes its sense, since the tempter would not have risked an application open to challenge; his fault was the purpose, and the clause he left out.

themes: There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling.
For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.
They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.
Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet.
Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name.
He shall call upon me, and I will answer him: I will be with him in trouble; I will deliver him, and honour him.
With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation.
